<description>
{
 "summary": "Adds a weekly GitHub Actions workflow and helper script (`contrib/devtools/check-code-signing-certificates.py`) to monitor the expiration and revocation status of the Windows code signing certificate. The script verifies the certificate's key usage extensions, checks its CRL distribution point for revocation, and warns when the certificate is within 90 days of expiry. When a certificate requires replacement, the CI job files a GitHub issue unless a report for that certificate state already exists.",
 "problem": "Bitcoin Core has no automated tracking for code signing certificate expiration or revocation. Maintainers currently rely on release candidate cycles for signers to notice that certificates have expired, which risks unexpected release delays if an emergency or off-schedule patch release is needed.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"Currently we have no automation in place to check that our code signing certificates are not expired or close to expiry. We have previously 'relied on Release Candidates' as a dry-run for codesigners to realise that a certificate has expired and have time to fix it.\"",
  "PR description: \"'Noticing during RC cycle' also might not be appropriate in the future if we release more bugfix minor/patch releases on short notice.\""
 ],

<category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.

Tools that operators and downstream projects depend on first: seed

developer productivity tools that many contributors use. Then niche or
single-user scripts, which rank low regardless of size.
